presentingComplaint: Nausea, right upper quadrant discomfort and dark urine 3 days after a staggered paracetamol overdose taken for dental pain.
history: 34-year-old woman presents with 2 days of anorexia, nausea, malaise and vague right upper quadrant discomfort. She admits taking approximately 6-8 g/day of paracetamol over the preceding 4-5 days for severe dental pain, exceeding the recommended maximum, and reports moderate alcohol use during the same period. No prescription drugs, no herbal/ayurvedic supplements, no recent travel, no risk factors for viral hepatitis, no prior liver disease. She now notices darkening of the urine. No fever, no rash, no arthralgia.
examination: Alert and oriented, mildly icteric sclerae. Mild tender hepatomegaly with right upper quadrant tenderness; Murphy sign negative. No stigmata of chronic liver disease (no spider naevi, no palmar erythema, no ascites), no asterixis, no organomegaly beyond liver edge, no lymphadenopathy, no rash. Pertinent negatives: no fever, no encephalopathy, no bleeding.

labs.Paracetamol level: detectable, taken outside nomogram-interpretable window (staggered ingestion)

imaging: Abdominal ultrasound: normal liver echotexture, patent hepatic and portal vessels, no biliary dilatation, no gallstones, no ascites — excludes obstruction and confirms non-cholestatic pattern.
stewardship: not applicable — non-infective. Management is N-acetylcysteine, not antibiotics.
contraindications: Avoid further hepatotoxins including additional paracetamol and alcohol
Caution with sedatives that could mask evolving encephalopathy
Anaphylactoid reactions possible with IV N-acetylcysteine infusion
edgeCases: Staggered/therapeutic-excess ingestion makes the Rumack-Matthew nomogram uninterpretable — treat on the basis of dose history and transaminases rather than a single level
Alcohol and fasting induce CYP2E1 and deplete glutathione, lowering the toxic threshold
A rising INR and bilirubin with falling transaminases can signal progression to acute liver failure — apply King's College criteria
expectedMaiK: Marked hepatocellular transaminitis (ALT/AST in thousands) with near-normal ALP after documented paracetamol excess points to drug-induced hepatotoxicity; start N-acetylcysteine promptly and serially monitor INR, bilirubin, creatinine and pH for evolving acute liver failure using King's College criteria.
expectedNextQuestions: Exact total paracetamol dose, timing and whether ingestion was staggered or single-time
Concurrent alcohol, herbal/OTC supplements, and any other hepatotoxic medications
expectedInvestigations: Serum paracetamol level with timed sampling
Coagulation profile (INR), venous lactate and arterial pH
Viral hepatitis serology and autoimmune screen to exclude alternatives
